Timeline · from Solon to 2007

The abolitions

The abolition of slavery as state policy, pursued on a global scale, was born in Atlantic societies in the 19th century. Most African, Ottoman and Arab abolitions were obtained under British or international pressure, sometimes very late.

  1. 6th c. BCEAthens · Solon bans the debt slavery of Athenians.
  2. 9 CEChina · Wang Mang abolishes slavery, restored in 12.
  3. 1102England · Slave trade banned.
  4. 1334Sweden · Slavery abolished.
  5. 1723-1730China · Yongzheng frees most hereditary servile groups.
  6. 1794France · Slavery abolished on February 4; the slave trade is reinstated by Bonaparte in 1802.
  7. 1801Korea · State nobi freed.
  8. 1807Great Britain · Slave trade abolished; the Royal Navy fights it until 1867.
  9. 1816Algiers · Bombarded by Lord Exmouth; European slaves freed.
  10. 1833Great Britain · Slavery abolished; £20 M paid to the owners.
  11. 1843British India · End of the legal recognition of slavery.
  12. 1848France · Final abolition (Victor Schœlcher). to be verified
  13. 1857Ottoman Empire · Ban on the trade in Black Africans, long poorly enforced.
  14. 1861Russia · Serfdom abolished.
  15. 1865United States · 13th Amendment. to be verified
  16. 1873Khiva · Abolition after the Russian conquest.
  17. 1888Brazil · Golden Law: the last abolition in the Americas. to be verified
  18. 1894Korea · Gabo Reform.
  19. 1897Zanzibar · Abolition, extended to concubines in 1909.
  20. 1901Northern Nigeria · End of the legal status of slavery in Sokoto.
  21. 1909-1910China · Official abolition.
  22. 1915Siam · Legal end, following the 1905 act.
  23. 1929Iran, Jordan · Abolition.
  24. 1942Ethiopia · Abolition by Haile Selassie.
  25. 1949-1952Kuwait, Qatar · Abolition.
  26. 1962Saudi Arabia, Yemen · Abolition.
  27. 1970Oman · Abolition under Sultan Qaboos.
  28. 1981Mauritania · Abolition by decree, without criminal penalties.
  29. 2007Mauritania · Slavery becomes a crime.

Two findings to keep side by side

A movement born in the West

The United Kingdom devoted considerable resources to fighting the slave trade: from 1808 to 1867, the West Africa Squadron captured about 1,600 ships and freed about 150,000 Africans. Kaufmann and Pape see it as "by far the most costly international moral action in modern history."

Paid to the masters, not to the victims

The British and French abolitions compensated the owners, never the enslaved. In Haiti, it was the former slaves who paid an indemnity to the colonists, until 1921-1922. The fight against the slave trade also served to justify the colonization of Africa.
